prompt: According to the PAM 3-0702-01 statement on the EP slide, Electronic Protection safeguards friendly personnel, facilities and equipment from the effects of what?
options: Adversary electronic attack, whether by jammers or false signals
Adversary and natural interference, excluding friendly emissions
Adversary intercept and direction finding of friendly emitters
Emissions in the spectrum, whether friendly, adversary or natural
explanation: Slides 7 and 25 quote PAM 3-0702-01: EP safeguards personnel, facilities and equipment from the effects of spectrum emissions, including friendly, adversary or natural electromagnetic interference. The option excluding friendly emissions is the closest distractor, but the quotation names friendly interference explicitly.

prompt: In a classroom duel, the enemy spot-jams our channel and our radios begin to hop. According to the example, what does the enemy do next?
options: Switches to direction finding of the hopping radios
Switches from spot jamming to barrage jamming
Lowers his power and masks with terrain
Switches the attack to our PACE alternate means
explanation: Slide 6 gives the example duel in which the enemy answers our hopping by switching to barrage jamming. Lowering power and masking with terrain is the closest distractor, but those are our next moves, not the enemy's.

prompt: According to the news slide, what did the Philippine Navy report in February 2024?
options: Direction finding had increased against ships' and land-based comms, mostly cellphones
Jamming had increased and affected ships' and land-based comms, mostly cellphones
Pilots were losing GPS on approach, so interference reports became mandatory
Command posts and drone teams were found by their emissions and hit by fires
explanation: Slide 5 reports that in February 2024 in the West Philippine Sea the Navy reported increased jamming that affected ships' and land-based comms, mostly cellphones. The GPS-on-approach option is the closest distractor, but that is the separate airport example, where the aviation authority now requires GNSS interference reports.

prompt: A section sends its situation report at the same minute every hour. Which change best applies the radio-discipline rule it is neglecting?
options: Shorten the report with brevity codes but keep the hourly schedule
Raise power for the hourly report so it is received first time
Add a radio check before each hourly report to confirm the net
Vary the report times so no fixed pattern forms
explanation: Slide 9 tells units to vary their routine, with no fixed report times or patterns. Shortening the report is the closest distractor, but it applies the short-transmissions rule and leaves the predictable schedule untouched.

prompt: A platoon leader worries the enemy can read what the platoon says on the net. Which group of measures answers that enemy question?
options: Emission control, low power and terrain masking
Secure mode, brevity codes, and saying less, less often
Frequency hopping, directional antennas and PACE alternate means
Hardening, shielding and attention to cable grounding
explanation: Slide 8 answers "Can I READ you?" with encryption in secure mode, brevity codes, and saying less, less often. The emission control group is the closest distractor, but Slide 8 assigns it to the "Can I FIND you?" question.

prompt: Where does the lesson place camouflage nets to block stray radiation from a directional antenna?
options: On the sides and back of the antenna
Across the front of the antenna
On the top and front of the antenna
Around the radio set but not the antenna
explanation: Slide 10 states that camouflage nets on the sides and back of directional antennas block stray radiation. Netting across the front is the closest distractor, but the front is where the wanted energy is aimed at your own station.

prompt: A signal platoon operates near a town with busy commercial radio networks. Which approach best hides its military emissions according to the lesson?
options: Transmit in a steady, constant pattern so the traffic looks like background
Use a quiet band where military signals are the only ones present
Send traffic at fixed times when the commercial networks are busiest
Use the spectrum as nearby users do and avoid predictable report times
explanation: Slides 11 and 23 say busy civilian networks helped mask military signals, provided a unit avoids odd signals and predictable patterns. The fixed-times option is the closest distractor, but predictable report times are exactly what Slide 11 warns against.

prompt: Why were command posts high-payoff targets in the Ukraine lessons?
options: Their emissions were brief, weak and irregular
Their emissions were stationary and constant
Their radios could not hop or encrypt
Their antennas were mounted on hilltops
explanation: Slide 23 says command posts were high-payoff targets because their emissions were stationary and constant. The hilltop option is the closest distractor, because Slide 10 does warn that hilltops are easy to DF, but that is siting advice and not the reason the Ukraine slide gives.

prompt: A brigade at the field baseline EMCON learns that an attack has occurred. Which move follows from the EMCON table?
options: Move to EMCON 5, BLACK: isolate compromised systems
Move to EMCON 2, YELLOW: limit transmissions and watch power levels
Move to EMCON 4, RED: switch non-essential emitters off and use alternates
Stay at EMCON 3, AMBER: encrypt, hop and use directional antennas
explanation: Slide 12 sets EMCON 4 RED for when an attack has occurred, with non-essential emitters off and alternates used. EMCON 5 BLACK is the closest distractor, but it is for attacks that are under way and isolates compromised systems.

prompt: Which action belongs to EMCON 2, YELLOW?
options: Switch non-essential emitters off and use alternates
Encrypt, hop and turn unencrypted systems off
Carry on normal operations with encryption on
Limit transmissions and watch power levels
explanation: Slide 12 gives EMCON 2 YELLOW as a risk of attack, with limited transmissions and watched power levels. The encrypt-and-hop option is the closest distractor, but it describes EMCON 3 AMBER, the next level up in restriction.

prompt: A battalion is at the field baseline EMCON, and one legacy radio cannot encrypt. What does that level require for the legacy radio?
options: It keeps working, but only on short transmissions at low power
It keeps working, but only with a directional antenna
It is held back and used only as an alternate later
It is turned off, since unencrypted systems are off at EMCON 3
explanation: Slide 12 states that at EMCON 3 AMBER, the field baseline, systems that are not encrypted are switched off. Holding it as an alternate is the closest distractor, but using alternates is the EMCON 4 RED response to an attack that has already occurred.

prompt: Why does encryption alone not protect a link from jamming?
options: It protects whether the signal gets through, not what is said
It hides the transmitter's location but cannot hide the message
It protects what is said, not whether the signal gets through
It spreads the signal, which helps against detection but not jamming
explanation: Slides 14 and 25 explain that encryption protects what you say but does not stop jamming or hide your location. The first reversed option is the closest distractor, but whether the signal gets through is the job of the anti-jam measures.

prompt: What does spread spectrum do, as the lesson describes it?
options: It spreads the signal so it is harder to detect and jam
It encrypts the signal so the enemy hears only gibberish
It concentrates the signal on one clear channel for better range
It switches to an alternate means when the net is jammed
explanation: Slide 13 says spread spectrum spreads the signal so it is harder to detect and jam. The encryption option is the closest distractor, but gibberish for the enemy is the result of encryption on Slide 14, not of spreading the signal.

prompt: A platoon is issued Combat Net Radio System sets, and a signaller prefers a fixed channel for clarity. Which instruction follows from the lesson?
options: Stay on a fixed channel until jamming is confirmed, then use hop mode
Use hop mode on the alternate net but a fixed channel on the primary
Use hop mode; PA tactical radios are required to have hopping and encryption
Use secure mode alone, since hopping adds no anti-jam value
explanation: Slide 13 says PA tactical radios, including the Combat Net Radio System, are required to have hopping and encryption and should be used in hop mode. The secure-mode-alone option is the closest distractor, but Slide 14 says encryption does not stop jamming, so hopping still matters.

prompt: A signaller disconnects the antenna during a noisy spell, and the noise stays. What does the quick test suggest?
options: Jamming or interference is arriving from outside
Terrain or antenna direction is involved
The radio, its cables or its power should be suspected
A friendly generator nearby is the cause
explanation: Slide 15 says that if the noise stays with the antenna disconnected, the signaller should suspect the radio, cables or power. The outside-source option is the closest distractor, but it is the conclusion drawn only when the noise drops.

prompt: Which observation does the lesson list among the signs of jamming?
options: The battery indicator drops after long use
The squelch opens although no one is talking
Signals fade only when the vehicle is behind a hill
One cable connector shows signs of corrosion
explanation: Slide 15 lists steady noise, tones, squelch opening with no one talking, broken voice or data, every station dropping at once, and GPS jumps or freezes. The hill option is the closest distractor, but fading behind terrain is one of the causes to rule out before blaming the enemy (Slide 4).

prompt: A signaller has kept operating on a noisy net without announcing the jamming. What does the reaction sequence call for next?
options: Check the equipment: antenna, cables, battery, settings and fills
Adjust by raising power briefly or moving behind cover
Report to the higher HQ by an alternate means
Go to the alternate frequency or means at once
explanation: Slide 16 puts the equipment check at step 2, after keeping operating and before adjusting. Adjusting is the closest distractor, but it is step 3 and only makes sense once a fault has been ruled out.

prompt: A section's primary hop-and-secure radio net is jammed, and it has a written PACE plan. What should the section do?
options: Jump to the emergency means first, to avoid being located
Keep waiting on the primary until the jamming stops
Go straight to the contingency means, since the alternate may also be jammed
Move to the alternate at the agreed trigger, as rehearsed
explanation: Slide 18 tells units to rehearse the switch and know the trigger, with the alternate following the primary. Going straight to the contingency means is the closest distractor, but it skips a step of the plan without a stated trigger.

prompt: What do CRPA antennas do for GPS protection?
options: Detect spoofed time and correct the clock
Null out jammers arriving at the receiver
Cross-check the fix against map and compass
Hide the receiver from enemy direction finding
explanation: Slide 19 states that CRPA antennas null out jammers. Detecting spoofed time is the closest distractor, but the slide handles spoofing through cross-checks against map, compass and terrain and not through the antenna.

prompt: At a command post, two radios sited together interfere with each other because they use the same frequencies. Which measure from the lesson addresses this?
options: Add shielding, filtering and grounding to both sets
Move both sets to a higher EMCON level
Separate the antennas and use only the frequencies assigned by the S6
Switch both sets to secure mode
explanation: Slide 20 under compatibility says to separate antennas, not co-site on the same frequencies, and use only the frequencies assigned by the S6. Shielding and grounding is the closest distractor, but that is hardening, which protects equipment from damaging energy rather than managing friendly emitters.

prompt: Which checks does the lesson say to make on every setup to confirm hardening?
options: Cable shielding, connectors and grounding
Assigned frequencies, antenna separation and co-siting
Hop pattern, error correction and secure mode
Power level, antenna direction and skyline placement
explanation: Slide 20 says to check cable shielding, connectors and grounding on every setup. The assigned-frequencies option is the closest distractor, but it is the compatibility check kept for spectrum management with the S6.

prompt: Which sensor ECCM technique squeezes a long, coded pulse on receive to give range detail and anti-jam margin?
options: Pulse compression
Frequency agility
Sidelobe blanking
Low-probability-of-intercept waveforms
explanation: Slide 21 describes pulse compression as a long, coded pulse squeezed on receive for range detail and anti-jam margin. Frequency agility is the closest distractor, but it changes frequency from pulse to pulse instead of reshaping the received pulse.
